{{Short description|Concept in feng shui}}
'''Dragon veins''' ({{lang-zh|link=no|龍脈/龙脉}}) or '''dragon's lines/tracks''' are a concept in [[Feng Shui]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web | title=The Basic Principles of Chinese Feng Shui | url=https://keatschinese.com/china-culture-resources/the-basic-principles-of-chinese-feng-shui/ }}</ref> It refers to channels of energy flowing through [[mountain range]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Feng Shui site selection: where the dragon stops: Anne Hansley suggests an ancient formula for auspicious home siting. |work= Free Online Library |url=https://www.thefreelibrary.com/Feng+Shui+site+selection:+where+the+dragon+stops:+Anne+Hansley...-a087703743 |access-date=2023-05-17 }}</ref> They are underground channels of [[Qi]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2019-02-04 |title=Dragons of the East and West: Feng Shui for Modern Living |url=https://www.fengshui.net/allied-interests/dragons-of-the-east-and-west-5646/ |access-date=2023-10-17 |language=en-GB}}</ref> According to some traditional religions, it is forbidden to destroy them, as this may cause negative consequences or disturbances.<ref name=":0" /> It has developed a metaphorical meaning of any critical infrastructure in the modern day such as the [[Qinghai–Tibet railway]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2022-01-09 |title=What is Dragon Vein? It is said that China has 3 large dragon veins |url=https://www.laitimes.com/en/article/1qr51_1x191.html |access-date=2023-05-17 |website=laitimes |language=en}}</ref>

The 1857 Feng Shui observation diary identified several sites in the Makija Hamlet, [[Okinawa Prefecture|Okinawa]], such as Uinu Utaki and Nuru Dunchi, believed to be connected to these dragon veins.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Bixia |last2=Nakama |first2=Yuei |date=2011 |title=A Feng Shui landscape and Tree Planting with explanation based on Feng Shui Diaries: A case study of Mainland Okinawa, Japan |journal=Worldviews |volume=15 |issue=2 |pages=168–184 |doi=10.1163/156853511X577475 |jstor=43809440 |issn=1363-5247}}</ref>

Qi forces vary in quality and quantity and move through the earth along "veins", referred to as "longmai" or "dragon veins". These veins concentrate at nodal points known as "caverns". While the forces are intangible, the network of veins can be inferred from topographical features.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last=Tsu |first=Timothy |date=1997 |title=Geomancy and the Environment in Premodern Taiwan |journal=Asian Folklore Studies |volume=56 |issue=1 |pages=65–77 |doi=10.2307/1178788 |jstor=1178788 |issn=0385-2342}}</ref>

After death, people are often buried next to Dragon veins.<ref>{{Cite book |chapter-url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv2rb761z.12 |access-date=2023-10-18 |jstor=j.ctv2rb761z.12 |language=en |chapter=Of Souls and Spirits |last1=Kipnis |first1=Andrew B. |title=The Funeral of Mr. Wang |date=2021 |pages=111–128 |publisher=University of California Press |isbn=9780520381971 |jstor-access=free }}</ref>

== History ==
During the [[Tang dynasty|Tang era]] (618-907), an "inspector of qi" or geomancer was sent by the court to the southwest in search of locations with "royal qi," a term indicating sites of special significance. This geomancer discovered the Coiled Dragon Mountain, which was believed to pulsate with a high concentration of "royal qi." Subsequently, the emperor directed people to settle in the area. Legends state that as the Baoning region developed, the mountain's features were shaped, and water sprang from it as if it were blood. The mountain's topography played a crucial role in defining the Baoning area, with the Coiled Dragon Mountain guarding its northern entrance. Geographically, the Dragon vein of the Coiled Dragon Mountain was central to the region's fengshui, a concept in which mountains or watersheds are believed to pulse with vital energy or "qi."<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Brown |first=Tristan G. |date=2019 |title=A Mountain of Saints and Sages: Muslims in the Landscape of Popular Religion in Late Imperial China |journal=T'oung Pao |volume=105 |issue=3/4 |pages=437–491 |doi=10.1163/15685322-10534P06 |jstor=26846140 |s2cid=211665547 |issn=0082-5433|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The Coiled Dragon Mountain's name draws from the geomantic image of a coiled [[Black Tortoise|Xuanwu]], a Chinese mythological figure visualized as a serpent wrapped around a tortoise. This figure is associated with the northern direction and the water element. The mountain held particular geomantic importance, with the Pavilion of Lingering Illumination positioned at the end of the Dragon vein.<ref name=":3" />

This mountain's significance was recognized in imperial times, especially during the [[Ming dynasty]]. The Pavilion of Lingering Illumination, located on the mountain, became an emblem of its powerful geomantic influence, and was supported by imperial patronage. Local elite and officials celebrated the shrine's geomantic powers and general significance, linking it to larger Chinese cosmological beliefs. For instance, some scholars believed the mountain was connected to the Dragon veins of the [[Kunlun Mountains]], a legendary location in Central Asia. During certain examination periods, scholars would visit the mountain's shrine hoping for academic success, and provincial officials acknowledged the shrine's societal contributions.<ref name=":3" />

Prominent poets, like Xie Jialin from the [[Qing dynasty|Qing era]], lauded the shrine's stature, acknowledging its imperial support and the presence of a significant religious figure. They believed the shrine held particular importance for the local community.<ref name=":3" />

=== Taiwan ===
In pre-twentieth-century [[Taiwan]], this geomantic practice influenced how the environment was perceived and treated. For instance, excavation activities that might disrupt a dragon vein were seen as detrimental. In 1815, a large-scale excavation in communal territories near the county seat was protested for damaging the landscape's "dragon body". Another case from 1895 illustrates a land lease that expressly prohibited coal mining due to its potential to harm the dragon vein; here, the justification was geomantic, not economic.<ref name=":2" />

Cases also highlighted the community's interest in preserving geomantically efficacious land. A market near [[Danshui]] in 1867 saw community leaders seek an official ban on excavation of a dragon vein, as they believed it brought prosperity to the town. While there were tensions between geomantic considerations and utilitarian or economic approaches to the land, there were instances of compromise. An 1857 land deed, for example, allowed the use of a geomantic site for vegetable farming but prohibited its conversion into rice paddies. This illustrates an effort to balance both the geomantic significance and economic use of the environment.<ref name=":2" />

== Effect on archaeology ==
During his archaeological endeavors in [[Mainland Southeast Asia]], [[Olov Janse]] encountered a tomb in [[Ho Chung]] on the [[Sai Kung Peninsula]] believed by locals to be under the protection of a dragon, representing a dragon vein. Initially skeptical of these beliefs, Janse came to understand the site's cultural significance. To gain excavation permissions, he engaged with local traditions and assured the community that his team would respect the dragon vein by limiting their excavation depth. Consequently, the villagers granted him the necessary consent.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Källén |first1=Anna |chapter=Euphoria: Indochina, October 1934–May 1935 |date=2021 |chapter-url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv26qjj9f.12 |title=The Archaeologist In-Between |pages=140–179 |access-date=2023-10-18 |series=Olov Janse, 1892–1985 |publisher=Kriterium |isbn=978-91-7061-305-0 |last2=Hegardt |first2=Johan|jstor=j.ctv26qjj9f.12 }}</ref>
